INTRODUCTION
Adolescent dating violence victimization is a widespread 
and pressing public health concern, with significant implications for youth development and long-term well-being. 
National estimates indicate that approximately 1 in 3 adolescents in the United States experiences some form of 
physical, emotional, or psychological violence within a 
dating relationship (Clayton et al., 2023), and this issue has 
long been recognized as a matter of national urgency (Leen 
et al., 2013). A growing body of research has linked adolescent dating violence victimization to a range of immediate 
negative outcomes which may disrupt physical, emotional, 
and social development. Victims are more likely to experience symptoms of depression and anxiety, often rooted 
in the trauma and diminished self-worth associated with

Abstract
Adolescent dating violence victimization is a prevalent public health issue with potential 
long-term consequences, yet little is known about its impact on different forms of adult 
violence. This study investigated the long-term association between adolescent dating 
violence victimization and violence involvement in adulthood, differentiating between 
intimate partner violence (IPV) and non-intimate partner violence (non-IPV), as well 
as victimization and perpetration. It also examined whether these associations vary by 
gender and race/ethnicity. This study used data from the National Longitudinal Study 
of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health) (N=2164). Sibling fixed effects logistic 
regression models were employed to control for unobserved family-level heterogeneity. 
Interaction terms tested for gender and racial/ethnic differences. Adolescent dating 
violence victimization was significantly associated with increased odds of non-IPV 
perpetration (OR=2.387, 95% CI [1.183, 4.815]) and IPV victimization (OR=1.880, 95% CI 
[1.266, 2.792]) in adulthood. When disaggregating by type, psychological dating violence 
victimization was linked to higher odds of non-IPV perpetration and IPV victimization, 
whereas physical dating violence victimization was more strongly associated with 
both IPV victimization and perpetration. No significant patterns of gender or racial/
ethnic heterogeneity were observed. Findings highlight the developmental continuity 
of violence and the importance of distinguishing between violence types and roles. 
Adolescent dating violence victimization, particularly in psychological and physical 
forms, poses a significant long-term risk for adult violence involvement. These results 
underscore the need for early prevention efforts and relationship education that address 
both victimization and perpetration in diverse contexts.

abusive relationships (Baiden et  al.,  2021; Van Ouytsel

et al., 2017). Exposure to dating violence is also linked to 
increased substance use, as adolescents may turn to alcohol or drugs to manage emotional distress or relational 
turmoil (Piolanti & Foran, 2022a). Academically, affected 
youth tend to show reduced school engagement, lower academic performance, and higher rates of absenteeism, reflecting the broader toll of interpersonal violence on their 
functioning and well-being (Taquette & Monteiro, 2019). 
Despite substantial evidence on these short-term effects, 
less is known about the long-term consequences of adolescent dating violence victimization, particularly whether 
such experiences contribute to continued involvement in 
violence into adulthood.
A growing body of research suggests that adolescent dating violence victimization may serve as a critical precursor 
to violence experiences in adulthood, reflecting developmental continuity in interpersonal violence. Early exposure 
to dating violence can shape maladaptive relational patterns, normalize coercive or aggressive behaviors, and impair the development of healthy coping and communication 
skills (Capaldi et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2003). These patterns 
may become internalized and later manifest in adult relationships, increasing the likelihood of both revictimization 
in adult intimate partnerships and perpetration of violence 
in various social contexts. For instance, individuals who experience psychological or physical aggression in adolescence 
may carry forward distorted expectations about relationship 
dynamics, such as associating love with control or conflict, 
which can contribute to cycles of violence (Exner-Cortens 
et al., 2017). Empirical studies have shown that adolescent 
dating violence victimization is linked not only to poor 
mental health and substance use in young adulthood but 
also to elevated risks of intimate partner violence (IPV) victimization and perpetration years later (Johnson et al., 2015; 
Smith et al., 2003).
Despite existing evidence, several areas warrant further 
attention. First, distinguishing between types of violence 
outcomes—specifically, intimate partner violence (IPV) 
versus non-intimate partner violence (non-IPV), and victimization versus perpetration—is essential for developing

a more nuanced understanding of the long-term consequences of adolescent dating violence victimization (Kim 
et al., 2025). IPV occurs within emotionally significant and 
often interdependent relationships, where dynamics, such 
as attachment, power, and emotional investment shape 
both the experience and expression of violence (Capaldi 
et al., 2012; Exner-Cortens et al., 2023). In contrast, non-IPV 
typically involves acquaintances or strangers and may arise 
from different social, situational, or behavioral pathways, 
such as peer influence, impulsivity, or exposure to community violence (Siegel et  al., 2019). Likewise, differentiating 
between victimization and perpetration is important, as 
these roles may be driven by distinct underlying mechanisms—such as trauma, social learning, or deficits in selfregulation (Cui et al., 2013; Park & Kim, 2019). Treating all 
violence outcomes as a single, homogenous category risks 
obscuring meaningful variation in how adolescent dating 
violence victimization influences individuals over time.
Second, understanding of how the long-term consequences of adolescent dating violence victimization may 
differ by gender and race/ethnicity remains limited. Much 
of the existing literature has focused primarily on overall 
prevalence and short-term outcomes, often treating gender 
and racial/ethnic differences as secondary considerations 
or relying on subgroup analyses without sufficient statistical power (Hamby & Turner, 2013; Vagi et al., 2013). Some 
studies suggest that females are more likely to experience 
psychological and physical victimization, while males may 
be more likely to perpetrate violence; but findings are often 
inconsistent and may overlook important contextual or intersectional factors (Foshee et al., 2010; Spencer et al., 2016; 
Storer et al., 2021).
Meanwhile, racial and ethnic minority youth—such as 
Black, Hispanic, and Asian adolescents—have been consistently found to exhibit heightened vulnerability both to

repeated exposure to victimization and to the victim-toperpetrator cycle (Kaukinen et  al.,  2015; Lo et  al.,  2020). 
They are more likely to encounter structural disadvantages 
that limit access to protective resources in the context of 
victimization, including legal safeguards, mental healthcare, and social support systems (Joo et  al.,  2024; Park & 
Kim, 2025; Weiss et al., 2017). Furthermore, environmental conditions such as relatively elevated rates of community violence, childhood maltreatment, and peer bullying 
may further compound their violence-related experiences 
(McNulty & Bellair, 2003; Rojas-Gaona et al., 2016; Spriggs 
et al., 2007). As a result, compared with White adolescents, 
dating violence victimization may be more readily internalized among youth of color, thereby increasing their 
subsequent risk of violence involvement. Despite this growing recognition of racial/ethnic diversity and structural 
inequalities in violence-related experiences in the U.S., 
few studies have examined how these broader conditions 
may interact with early dating violence victimization to 
shape adult outcomes (Barhight et  al., 2017; Campo-Tena, 
Larmour, Pereda, & Eisner, 2024).
Third, many studies examining the link between adolescent dating violence victimization and later outcomes 
rely on conventional regression models that adjust only 
for observable covariates. However, accounting for unobserved family heterogeneity is essential for accurately 
assessing the long-term consequences of adolescent 
dating violence victimization—yet, this critical source 
of bias has been largely overlooked in prior research 
(Fergusson et  al.,  2005; Moffitt,  2005). Conventional 
models often fail to account for unmeasured family-level 
factors such as parenting practices, family conflict, exposure to violence in the home, or inherited behavioral 
tendencies, all of which may influence both the likelihood 
of experiencing dating violence victimization in adolescence and the risk of violence involvement in adulthood

(Ackard & Eisenberg, 2024; Calvete et al., 2018). Ignoring 
these shared influences can lead to biased or overstated

associations (Park et  al.,  2023), thereby conflating the 
true effects of adolescent dating violence victimization 
with broader familial or environmental risks.
Using data from the National Longitudinal Study of 
Adolescent to Adult Health, this study investigates the longterm consequences of adolescent dating violence victimization by examining its association with multiple forms of 
violence involvement in adulthood. Specifically, this study 
distinguishes between IPV and non-IPV, as well as between 
victimization and perpetration. This study primarily aims 
to assess the independent influence of adolescent dating 
violence victimization on adult violence outcomes across 
different contexts and roles. To address potential bias from 
unobserved family-level confounders, we employ a sibling 
fixed effect model which leverages within-family variation. This approach may offer a more rigorous estimation 
compared with alternative methods that rely on betweenfamily variation, such as ordinary least squares (OLS) or 
mixed-effects models. In addition, interaction models assess 
whether these associations vary by gender or race/ethnicity. 
By addressing key methodological limitations and disaggregating violence outcomes, this study contributes to a deeper 
understanding of the developmental continuity of violence 
and offers valuable insights for designing prevention and 
intervention strategies tailored to diverse populations and 
relationship dynamics.
DATA AND METHOD
Data
This study draws on data from the National Longitudinal 
Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health), a 
nationally representative, school-based study designed to 
investigate the health-related trajectories of U.S. adolescents 
into adulthood. The baseline survey (Wave I) was conducted 
during the 1994–1995 academic year, targeting students 
enrolled in grades 7 through 12 (ages 12–21). Participants 
were subsequently followed over multiple waves: Wave 
II in 1996 (age 13–22), Wave III in 2001–2002 (ages 18–

26), Wave IV in 2008–2009 (ages 24–32), and Wave V in 
2016–2018 (ages 33–43). These follow-up waves capture 
developmental stages from adolescence into early adulthood, 
young adulthood, and full adulthood. Add Health is widely 
regarded for its methodological rigor and high retention 
rates, which range from 77.4% to 88.6% across waves 
(Harris et  al.,  2019). The dataset offers rich longitudinal 
data on social, behavioral, and relational domains, including 
detailed information on family structure, peer dynamics, 
educational and occupational transitions, and romantic and 
sexual partnerships. This makes Add Health uniquely suited 
for investigating long-term associations between adolescent 
dating violence and subsequent involvement in interpersonal 
or non-intimate violence, whether as a victim or perpetrator.
A distinguishing feature of Add Health is its oversampling of sibling pairs, enabling more robust controls for 
familial and genetic confounding. The present study focuses on a sibling subsample comprising 3666 individuals 
who were followed through Wave IV. From this group, we 
excluded 1502 respondents who had not reported any romantic relationships by Wave II, as our primary interest 
is in the longitudinal consequences of early dating experiences. The final analytic sample included 2164 individuals. 
To address missing data on key covariates—most notably, 
cognitive ability scores missing for 94 respondents—we employed multiple imputation using chained equations (MICE) 
in Stata version 18.5. Ten imputed datasets were generated, 
and all analytic models included imputed values to improve 
statistical precision and reduce bias (White et al., 2011). All 
participants (or their next of kin/caregiver) provided written informed consent in accordance with Add Health study 
protocols. As this research involves secondary analysis of deidentified, publicly available data, it was exempt from full 
review by an institutional review board.
Measures
Dependent variable
The primary outcome variable in this study, measured at 
Wave IV, is adult violence involvement, distinguished along 
two key dimensions: (1) the type of violence—IPV versus

non-IPV, and (2) the role—victimization versus perpetration.
IPV experiences were assessed during Wave IV for participants who reported being in a romantic relationship at 
the time. IPV victimization was measured using four items 
that asked how often, in the past 12months, a partner had: 
(1) slapped, hit, or kicked the respondent; (2) threatened violence, pushed or shoved them, or thrown something potentially harmful; (3) forced or insisted on sexual relations 
against their will; and (4) caused physical injuries, such 
as sprains, bruises, or cuts due to a physical altercation. 
Response options ranged from 0 (never) to 7 (more than 20 
times). For analytical purposes, responses from 1 to 7 were 
recoded as 1, indicating any occurrence of IPV victimization, while a response of 0 was coded as 0, reflecting no victimization. This resulted in a binary indicator capturing the 
presence or absence of IPV victimization in the past year. 
IPV perpetration was assessed using the same four behavioral items, rephrased to reflect the respondent's own actions 
toward their partner. Responses were coded in the same binary fashion to indicate whether the respondent had perpetrated any form of IPV in the preceding 12months.
In addition to IPV, non-IPV experiences were also 
captured in Wave IV, focusing on incidents that typically occur outside intimate relationships—often involving strangers, acquaintances, or occurring in public 
settings. Non-IPV victimization was assessed by asking respondents whether, in the past year, they had been 
the target of violence, including having a weapon (knife 
or gun) pulled on them, being shot or stabbed, slapped, 
hit, choked, kicked, or beaten up. A binary variable was

created, with 1 indicating any experience of such events 
and 0 indicating none. Non-IPV perpetration was measured using items that asked whether the respondent had, 
in the past 12 months, engaged in violent acts such as pulling a weapon on someone, stabbing or shooting someone,

taking part in a group fight, or getting into a serious physical fight. As with other outcomes, a binary variable was 
created to capture any instance of non-IPV perpetration 
during the reference period.
All violence outcome variables were dichotomized to indicate the presence or absence of each type of violence involvement (victimization or perpetration, IPV or non-IPV). 
This decision was guided by several methodological and 
substantive considerations. First, this approach aligns with 
standard practice in the violence literature, where binary 
indicators (e.g., any victimization vs. none) are commonly 
used to facilitate comparability across studies and to reflect 
the public health significance of experiencing any violence. 
Second, dichotomization facilitated the use of logistic regression models, which estimate the relative odds of violence 
involvement while controlling for unobserved family-level 
confounders through sibling fixed effects.
Independent variable
During Wave II, participants were asked to report 
up to three current or past romantic relationships. A 
relationship was considered romantic if it included 
affectionate behaviors—such as holding hands, kissing, or 
saying “I love you”—and was characterized by labels like 
“boyfriend” or “girlfriend.” For each reported relationship, 
participants indicated whether they had experienced any of 
five specific partner behaviors (coded 0 = “no,” 1 = “yes”): 
“publicly insulted you,” “swore at you,” “threatened you 
with physical violence,” “pushed or shoved you,” or “had 
something thrown at you.” The first three behaviors were 
drawn from the psychological aggression subscale of the 
Revised Conflict Tactics Scale (CTS2), while the last two 
were adapted from the physical assault subscale (Straus 
et  al.,  1996). A binary indicator for psychological dating 
violence victimization was created by coding respondents 
as 1 if they reported experiencing at least one of the three 
psychological aggression items. Similarly, physical dating 
violence victimization was coded as 1 if at least one of 
the two physical assault items was endorsed. An overall 
measure of adolescent dating violence victimization was

constructed and coded as 1 if the participant reported 
experiencing any of the five listed behaviors in any of their 
reported relationships.
Although Wave II includes respondents aged 13–22, about 
92% of the analytic sample were younger than 20, corresponding to adolescence in standard developmental frameworks. 
The small proportion of participants aged 20 or older can be 
considered late adolescents or emerging adults. Given this age 
distribution, we consider it appropriate to characterize the exposure as adolescent dating violence victimization.
Control variable
Recognizing that demographic factors are well-documented 
predictors of violence exposure (Napier et  al.,  2023), this 
study adjusted for a range of individual-level covariates assessed at Wave I. These included participants’ age, gender, 
race/ethnicity (categorized as White, Black, Hispanic, Asian, 
or Other), foreign-born status, first-born status, and cognitive ability, as measured by the Peabody Picture Vocabulary 
Test (PVT). To facilitate interpretation, PVT scores were 
standardized by subtracting the sample mean and dividing 
by the standard deviation. These background characteristics 
are known to influence adolescents’ vulnerability to violence 
and may also shape patterns of violence involvement later in 
life (Campo-Tena, Larmour, Ribeaud, & Eisner, 2024; Maas 
et al., 2010; Pereda et al., 2022). Moreover, we included the 
number of dating relationships as a covariate. This variable 
accounts for differences in opportunity for dating violence 
exposure, given prior evidence that having multiple relationships increases the likelihood of experiencing dating violence (Halpern et al., 2009). Including these covariates in the 
models helps reduce potential confounding and enhances 
the precision of estimates regarding the long-term association between adolescent dating violence and adult violence 
outcomes.
Analytic strategy
To examine the association between adolescent dating violence victimization and violence involvement in adulthood, 
we employed sibling fixed effects logistic regression models, 
which control for unobserved, time-invariant heterogeneity 
at the family level. Given that all outcome variables in this

study are binary indicators—reflecting whether respondents 
experienced or perpetrated violence in adulthood—logistic 
regression is an appropriate modeling choice. A key concern 
in observational studies is the presence of unmeasured confounding. In this context, unobserved family-level characteristics that are shared between siblings—such as common 
genetic predispositions, socioeconomic background, overall 
parenting practices, or early family-level adversity—may influence both adolescent dating violence victimization and 
adult violence outcomes. If left unaccounted for, such confounding can bias estimates of association. The sibling fixed 
effects approach addresses this issue by leveraging withinfamily variation, effectively holding constant all shared 
family-level characteristics (both observed and unobserved).

The term 𝜇f captures sibling fixed effects, thereby accounting

the sibling fixed effects approach is equivalent to estimating 
within-family differences, isolating the impact of dating violence victimization on later outcomes while holding constant 
all shared background factors. To address potential clustering 
of residuals within families, robust standard errors (𝜀if) were 
clustered at the family level. Accordingly, we conducted four 
main sibling fixed effects logistic regression models, each corresponding to each of the adult violence outcomes: non-IPV 
victimization, non-IPV perpetration, IPV victimization, and 
IPV perpetration.
We also conducted post hoc sensitivity analyses using

G*Power (version 3.1) to estimate the minimum detectable odds ratios at 80% power and α=.05, given our sample 
size (N=2164), exposure prevalence (31%), and the prevalence of each outcome. These analyses indicated that the 
study was powered to detect odds ratios of approximately 
1.42 or greater for non-IPV victimization, 1.54 for non-IPV 
perpetration, 1.33 for IPV victimization, and 1.38 for IPV 
perpetration.
To further explore potential heterogeneity in the relationship between adolescent dating violence and adult violence 
outcomes, we estimated interaction models that incorporate 
interaction terms between adolescent dating violence victimization (ADVif) and key demographic variables—specifically, gender and race/ethnicity—into the baseline sibling 
fixed effects model (Equation 1). These models allow us to 
assess whether the association between adolescent dating violence and later violence involvement differs systematically 
across subgroups. The conceptual framework of our analytic 
model is presented in Figure 1.
RESULTS
Table 1 presented the descriptive statistics for the analytic 
sibling sample used in this study (N = 2164). The dependent variables, measured at Wave IV, captured four types 
of violence experiences in adulthood. Approximately, 14% 
of respondents reported experiencing non-IPV victimization, while 8% reported engaging in non-IPV perpetration. 
In contrast, rates of IPV were higher: 26% experienced IPV 
victimization, and 18% reported perpetrating IPV. The 
key independent variable—adolescent dating violence, 
measured at Wave II—was reported by 31% of respondents. 
When disaggregated by type, 29% experienced psychological dating violence, and 11% experienced physical dating 
violence. Individual-level covariates measured at Wave I 
include demographic and background characteristics. The 
average age of respondents was 16.32 years (SD = 1.66), and 
45% were male. The sample was racially/ethnically diverse, with 59% identifying as White, 22% as Black, 14%

as Hispanic, 4% as Asian, and 1% as another racial/ethnic group. Additionally, 6% of the sample were foreignborn, and 40% were first-born children. Respondents 
reported an average of 1.34 dating relationships at Wave 
II (SD = 0.61).
Table 2 displayed the results from sibling fixed effects logistic regression models assessing the association between 
adolescent dating violence victimization and adult violence 
outcomes. Focusing first on non-IPV outcomes, the association with non-IPV victimization was not statistically 
significant (Column 1). In contrast, as shown in Column 
2, adolescent dating violence victimization was significantly associated with non-IPV perpetration in adulthood 
(OR=2.210, 95% CI [1.074, 4.548], p<.05) (Column 2), indicating that individuals exposed to dating violence victimization in adolescence were more than twice as likely to engage 
in violent acts outside of intimate relationships compared 
with their siblings who did not report such experiences.

Table 3 presented results for heterogeneity in the association between adolescent dating violence victimization 
and adult violence outcomes by gender (Panel A) and race/
ethnicity (Panel B). In Panel A, the interaction terms with 
gender across all violence outcomes were not statistically 
significant across any outcomes, suggesting that the associations between adolescent dating violence victimization 
and adult violence involvement did not differ meaningfully 
between males and females. Panel B explored racial and ethnic differences. Most interaction terms between adolescent 
dating violence victimization and racial/ethnic groups were 
not statistically significant, indicating relatively consistent 
effects across racial/ethnic subgroups. However, a notable 
exception was the significant interaction for “Others” (i.e., 
racial/ethnic groups not classified as White, Black, Hispanic, 
or Asian) in the IPV perpetration model (OR=3.276, 95%

CI [1.134, 9.460], p<.05), suggesting a stronger association 
between adolescent dating violence victimization and adult 
IPV perpetration for respondents in this category. However, 
this finding should be interpreted cautiously due to the small 
sample size within that subgroup.
Table 4 reported the associations between different types 
of adolescent dating violence victimization —psychological and physical—and violence involvement in adulthood. 
Psychological dating violence was significantly associated 
with non-IPV perpetration (OR=2.095, 95% CI [1.042, 
4.660], p<.05; Column 2) and IPV victimization (OR=1.543, 
95% CI [1.018, 2.462], p<.05; Column 3). These findings suggested that adolescents who had experienced psychological aggression in romantic relationships were over twice as 
likely to perpetrate non-IPV and about 50% more likely to be 
victimized by an intimate partner in adulthood, compared 
with their siblings who did not report such experiences. In 
contrast, physical dating violence showed associations with 
IPV outcomes, but not with non-IPV outcomes. As shown 
in Columns 3 and 4, physical dating violence was a significant risk factor for both IPV victimization (OR=1.930, 95% 
CI [1.005, 3.704], p<.05) and IPV perpetration (OR=2.263, 
95% CI [1.058, 4.842], p<.05), indicating that adolescents exposed to physical aggression in romantic relationships were 
nearly twice as likely to be victimized and more than twice 
as likely to perpetrate IPV in adulthood.

family-level confounders through sibling fixed effects 
models. Specifically, individuals who experienced dating 
violence during adolescence were more likely to perpetrate 
non-IPV and experience victimization in intimate relationships later in life. These findings align with and extend prior 
research suggesting that early exposure to relationship violence can disrupt normative developmental trajectories and 
contribute to the persistence of aggressive or victimization 
patterns across the life course (Park et al., 2018). Adolescence 
is a critical developmental window during which individuals 
form foundational interpersonal skills, emotional regulation 
capacities, and internal models of romantic relationships 
(Calvete et al., 2018; Lundgren & Amin, 2015). Exposure to 
violence during this stage can distort perceptions of healthy 
relationship norms, normalize coercive or abusive behaviors, and impair the ability to navigate conflict constructively (Capaldi et al., 2012; Jang et al., 2024). Prior research 
has shown that these early disruptions are associated with 
long-term consequences such as increased emotional dysregulation, hostile attribution biases, and the adoption of 
maladaptive coping mechanisms, all of which elevate the 
risk of future violence involvement—both as victim and perpetrator (Sumner et al., 2015).
An especially noteworthy pattern emerging from the 
analysis is that individuals who experienced dating violence 
during adolescence are more likely to experience victimization in intimate partner contexts (i.e., within the home); 
yet are more likely to perpetrate violence in non-intimate

settings (i.e., outside the home). This divergence in role 
and context suggests that adolescent dating violence victimization may shape not only the risk of future violence 
but also the relational dynamics and situational contexts 
in which that violence occurs. One possible interpretation 
is that early exposure to violence in romantic relationships 
contributes to the internalization of submissive or helpless 
roles in close, emotionally charged relationships, making 
individuals more vulnerable to revictimization in later intimate partnerships (Manchikanti Gómez, 2011). Conversely, 
the same individuals may externalize their distress or model 
learned aggressive behaviors in less emotionally intimate 
or more confrontational settings, leading to aggression 
or dominance-seeking behavior in public or peer-related 
environments (Capaldi et  al.,  2012; Esquivel-Santoveña 
et  al.,  2021). This dual outcome underscores the complex 
and context-dependent effects of adolescent dating violence 
victimization. Victimization in early relationships may undermine the development of healthy interpersonal boundaries and coping skills, contributing to a cycle of victimization 
in emotionally significant relationships (Moon et al., 2022). 
At the same time, these early experiences may cultivate generalized aggression, mistrust, or hypervigilance that manifests outwardly in social contexts perceived as threatening 
or competitive.
The present study found no consistent empirical evidence 
of gender- or racial/ethnic-based heterogeneity in the association between adolescent dating violence victimization 
and adult violence outcomes. Although prior research has 
suggested that the consequences of violence may vary by 
gender, with women more likely to experience victimization and men more likely to perpetrate violence (Hamby & 
Turner, 2013; Malhi et al., 2020)—the interaction models in 
this analysis revealed no statistically significant differences 
in effects between males and females. Similarly, despite 
well-documented racial and ethnic disparities in exposure 
to community violence and structural disadvantage (Joo 
et  al.,  2024; Rojas-Gaona et  al.,  2016), the associations between adolescent dating violence victimization and later

violence outcomes did not significantly differ across major 
racial/ethnic groups. Overall, nonsignificant interaction effects suggest that the long-term impact of adolescent dating 
violence victimization on adult violence involvement may 
operate similarly across gender and racial/ethnic lines, highlighting the pervasive and broadly distributed nature of its 
consequences.
Another interesting finding from this study is the distinctive role of physical dating violence in increasing the 
risk of later violence outcomes. Specifically, physical dating violence victimization in adolescence was significantly 
associated with both IPV victimization and perpetration 
in adulthood, but showed no significant relationship with

either non-IPV victimization or perpetration. This pattern 
suggests that physical aggression experienced within early

romantic relationships may have a relationship-specific impact, shaping how individuals engage in or respond to conflict within future intimate partnerships. The absence of an 
association with non-IPV outcomes implies that the effects 
of physical dating violence victimization are not necessarily 
generalized to broader social interactions but are more likely 
to manifest within the emotionally intimate and often highstakes context of adult romantic relationships. This may be 
because physical dating violence victimization during adolescence disrupts normative expectations of safety, communication, and boundaries in intimate settings, potentially 
fostering cycles of both victimization and aggression that 
are contextually bound to romantic or domestic dynamics 
(Stith et al., 2004).
This study makes several important theoretical and methodological contributions to the literature on the long-term 
violence outcomes of adolescent dating violence victimization. Theoretically, the findings support developmental and 
life course perspectives that emphasize how early interpersonal experiences—particularly those involving violence—
can shape later behavioral patterns and relational dynamics 
(Littman & Paluck, 2015). By demonstrating that adolescent 
dating violence victimization is associated with both victimization and perpetration in adulthood, particularly in 
intimate contexts, the study reinforces models of behavioral continuity and cumulative disadvantage, suggesting 
that early adverse experiences cascade into long-term relational and psychosocial risks (Littman & Paluck,  2015). 
Additionally, by disaggregating violence outcomes into IPV 
and non-IPV, as well as victimization and perpetration, the 
study provides a more nuanced understanding of how adolescent experiences may influence distinct forms and roles 
in adult violence. Methodologically, the study advances 
the field by employing sibling fixed effects logistic regression models, a rigorous design that controls for all shared 
family-level confounders—such as overall parenting practices, household environment, and common genetic predispositions—that could bias associations in conventional 
observational studies.
Despite its strengths, this study has several limitations 
that warrant consideration. First, although the sibling 
fixed effects approach controls for all unobserved confounders shared between siblings, it does not account for

individual-specific unobserved factors, such as personality traits, peer influences, or unmeasured life events, 
which may also affect both adolescent dating violence 
victimization and adult outcomes. Second, the reliance on 
self-reported data may introduce social desirability bias, 
particularly regarding sensitive topics like IPV or perpetration. Such tendencies may contribute in part to the 
relatively low prevalence of adult violence involvement 
observed in our analytic sample. This limitation should 
be considered when interpreting our findings, as low outcome prevalence may reduce the statistical power of our 
models and lead to underestimation of associations.
Third, the analytic sample was restricted to sibling pairs 
in which at least one respondent reported having been in 
a romantic relationship by Wave II. As such, the generalizability of the findings may be limited with respect to 
only children or adolescents who initiated romantic relationships after Wave II. Given potential variation in both 
the risks and consequences of dating experiences based on 
family structure and the developmental timing of relationship initiation (Spencer et al., 2020), future research would 
benefit from examining whether the observed associations hold across adolescents with different sibling compositions and romantic relationship trajectories. Finally, 
the measures of dating violence victimization, although 
based on validated scales, may not capture the full range 
of experiences—such as coercive control, stalking, or digital abuse—that are increasingly recognized as components 
of dating violence. In particular, given the growing role 
of social media and online communication in shaping 
interpersonal dynamics during adolescence (RodríguezdeArriba et al., 2021; Thulin et  al., 2022), the absence of 
data on digital interaction may limit the extent to which 
this study reflects the contexts in which dating violence 
occurs. Future research that incorporates digital dimensions of dating violence victimization may provide more 
comprehensive insights into its long-term implications for 
violence involvement.
The findings of this study carry important policy implications. The demonstrated long-term association between 
adolescent dating violence victimization and adult violence

outcomes underscores the need for both universal prevention programs and early targeted interventions for dating 
violence victims. In particular, school-based interventions 
that promote healthy relationship skills, emotional regulation, and nonviolent conflict resolution among adolescents 
may be effective not only in reducing the risk of dating violence itself, but also in interrupting its entrenchment into 
adult involvement in violence (Finnie et  al.,  2022; Flores 
Morales et al., 2022; Jang & Kim, 2023; Lee & Wong, 2022). 
In parallel, social norms and institutional infrastructures 
must be strengthened to support the early identification of 
dating violence and to ensure timely responses across family, school, and community systems. These may include 
confidential reporting systems, coordinated mental health 
services, and community outreach efforts aimed at engaging at-risk youth (Doucette et al., 2021; Moore et al., 2015; 
Sharkey et al., 2017).
Additionally, given that both psychological and physical forms of dating violence are associated with long-term 
harm, policies and interventions should not focus exclusively on physical aggression. While substantial progress has 
been made in developing and evaluating programs targeting 
physical dating violence, effective interventions that address 
psychological dimensions—such as emotional and verbal abuse—remain comparatively underdeveloped (Arrojo 
et al., 2024; Piolanti & Foran, 2022b). Based on the recognition of the enduring consequences of non-physical forms of 
dating violence, the targeted strategies that respond to their

the distinct pattern wherein adolescent dating violence
